title: $300,000 in Cisco, IBM and Microsoft Could Pay You $5,150 a Year
detail:
$300,000 in Cisco, IBM and Microsoft Could Pay You $5,150 a Year

IBM

Quick Read

Splitting $300,000 evenly across Microsoft and IBM, plus Cisco, generates about $5,150 a year in dividends, a blended yield near 2%.

Microsoft yields under 1% but raised its quarterly dividend 8% and pays out only about 23% of earnings.

IBM pays the richest yield at roughly 3% and has paid dividends since 1916, though dividends eat 60% of free cash flow.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Plenty of retirees still think of tech stocks as growth plays that pay nothing while you wait. That view is out of date. Three of the biggest names in enterprise technology send cash to shareholders every quarter, and they have a long record of raising those payments.

raisbeckfoto / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images

A $300,000 investment, split into $100,000 in each of these three dividend payers, would produce about $5,150 in annual passive income, or more than $5,000 a year. That is modest for the money involved. This group appeals because the payout can grow fast, is well covered, and has reliably kept coming. Yields below are forward yields.

Microsoft Pays the Smallest Yield but Delivers the Fastest Raises

Stock #3: Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT)

Yield: 0.69%

Shares for $100,000: 176.02

Annual Passive Income: ~$690

Microsoft runs Azure, Microsoft 365, Windows, Xbox, and LinkedIn. Its yield is tiny because the stock has risen so far, giving it a market cap of about $4.02T. The dividend growth is where it stands out. The quarterly payout rose from $0.91 to $0.98, a 7.7% increase, and has risen every year since 2005 on the provided record.

Coverage is very strong. The $3.92 forward dividend works out to about 23% of fiscal 2026 EPS of $17.28. The main risk is spending: Microsoft expects calendar-year capex of approximately $170 billion, and free cash flow was $18.6 billion last quarter even though operating cash flow came in at $58 billion.

Cisco Turns an AI Networking Boom Into Steady Dividend Increases

Stock #2: Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO)

Yield: 1.73%

Annual Passive Income: ~$1,730

Cisco sells networking, security, collaboration, and observability products plus services. Cisco is a mature, cash-heavy business, so it returns a larger share of its profit to shareholders. The company raised its dividend for the 15th consecutive year in fiscal 2026, and the quarterly payment now stands at $0.42.

title: EU sues IBM over airport border delays
detail:
EU sues IBM over airport border delays
Hans van Leeuwen
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 8:50 AM CST 2 min read
IBM
LDO.MI
Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Challenges caused by the new smart border system resulted in slow-moving airport customs queues - Anadolu via Getty Images/Dursun Aydemir

The EU is suing IBM and two major European tech firms over the troubled rollout of the bloc's new smart border system.

The Entry/Exit System (EES), which requires fingerprints and facial scans, caused long queues at EU airports over the summer, prompting uproar among passengers and airlines.

The system was plagued by malfunctioning fingerprint scanners and automatic kiosks, as well as cumbersome checking procedures. With passengers languishing in slow-moving customs queues, some flights were forced to take off half-empty.

EU-Lisa, the agency that manages bloc-wide IT systems, has launched a challenge against EES's implementation partners: IBM, Italian defence contractor Leonardo and French tech firm Atos.

The agency said its lawsuit, filed in Estonia last December, had "activated the available contractual and legal remedies to protect its financial interests".

That followed "various delays in the delivery of the EES by a contracting consortium".

The lawsuit, first reported by the Financial Times, relates to alleged delays and budget blowouts in developing the system, rather than the more recent airport chaos.

EU-Lisa said: "The proceedings concern the system's development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES is fully operational."

The EU previously fined the consortium for missing delivery deadlines on the €142m (£118m) contract, whose cost had risen to €212m by 2021. According to the Financial Times, the companies disputed the fines, in some cases blaming the Covid-19 pandemic.

The system applies to citizens of any country outside the EU and its wider Schengen area, a visa-free travel zone that also includes Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

Anyone entering the bloc for the first time since the system went live is supposed to provide fingerprints and a facial image, allowing the bloc to track people's movements and identify visa over-stayers.

The EES had been supposed to start in 2022 after a five-year gestation, but was only launched in October last year.

Countries faced a September deadline this year to deploy the system.

But some – including France, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Portugal, the Netherlands, Greece, Malta and Switzerland – are reportedly still relying on their legacy systems at least part of the time, with tacit permission from Brussels.

The contract with Atos, IBM and Leonardo expired last year, and a new consortium has taken over. All three companies were contacted for comment.

The system's proponents say it is successfully pinpointing thousands of unauthorised arrivals and over-stayers.

Some teething problems have been blamed on the EU having to coordinate the tech with each country's existing software and hardware.

We just published the list of the 10 Worst Dow Stocks To Buy, and IBM (NYSE:IBM) ranks 9th on this list.

Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, as the leading AI chipmaker fell 9% to pace Dow decliners and another chip designer plunged 17%, the outlet reported.

The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped nearly 1,600 points after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. Even so, the blue-chip index finished Thursday just 1.9% below its record closing high of 54,349 from early August, according to Yahoo Finance.

IBM (IBM): Software Is Speeding Up, Yet Analysts' Average Upside Is 5%
The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares. One household consumer brand has divided opinion lately, and we covered why a well-known TV host is staying away from the sneaker maker after losing money on it.

On Thursday that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular, according to Yahoo Finance. Data center power and infrastructure stocks fell by double digits, and the Nasdaq 100 was recently more than 10% below its October closing high.

The reversal was fast. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years, Yahoo Finance reported on November 5. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why a billionaire money manager and a TV host both still like the iPhone maker.

The stronger jobs data lifted Treasury yields and kept Federal Reserve policy at the center of market attention, Reuters reported on November 6, as the price-weighted index of 30 major U.S. companies held roughly flat.

IBM's average upside potential, based on analysts' average price target, is 5%. It has a short interest of 2.11% and had 74 hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026.
